A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–C are readable and support comparison despite substantial rewriting and expansion.

before.justification: Section 5 and Table 2 report original transformer recognition experiments, including in-distribution and out-of-distribution accuracies across five seeds. Appendix C describes data generation and training.

after.justification: Section 5 and Table 2 report original experiments comparing fixed-depth, looped, and looped-and-padded transformers, with maximum accuracies across five seeds. Appendix C supplies experimental settings.

M1.justification: The recognition strategies remain, but construction components change. Appendix B replaces Gorn-address arithmetic for binarization with item-and-chain-index keys and active-edge ranking. The pebble evaluator also revises its handling of constant propagators.

E1.justification: Section 5 and Table 2 add Balanced Counting as an evaluated language and remove Marked Palindrome. Binary Palindrome, Dyck(1), Dyck(2), and both BFVP notations remain. Balanced Counting previously appeared only as a theoretical example.

E2.justification: Table 2 expands the fixed-depth versus looping-only comparison into a three-way comparison including looping with O(N) padding. V3 explicitly uses the retained looping-only model as a baseline for the padded variant.

E3.justification: Appendix C changes the maximum training/test lengths from 40/80 to 50/500, substantially revising the length-generalization setting. Table 2 adds an O(N)-padded condition. Dataset sizes remain one million training and 2,000 test samples, and the stated parameter budget and optimizer settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Table 2 newly compares looping alone with looping plus padding, testing padding's incremental contribution. V2 examined looping and length generalization without this padding comparison. No separate sensitivity sweep or error analysis is added.

E5.justification: V2 reports means and standard deviations across seeds; v3 replaces these with the maximum accuracy across five seeds and removes dispersion reporting. Appendix C retains five seeds in both versions, so this is a substantial reporting change rather than a documented increase in runs.

E6.justification: Table 2 replaces the empirical results under changed settings and aggregation. For example, v2's postfix BFVP out-of-distribution fixed/looped means are 0.87±0.01 and 0.91±0.01; v3 reports best accuracies of 67/75/75 for fixed/looped/looped-and-padded models. Balanced Counting results are added and Marked Palindrome results disappear. These are not same-setting performance changes.

T1.justification: V3 corrects the centroid statement from two resulting trees to components and revises the runtime bound from log(n)+O(1) for all inputs to 2 ceil(log2(2N))+O(1) for member strings. Appendix B adds substantial induction arguments, construction invariants, and resource accounting. It also corrects the postfix negation definition while retaining the principal asymptotic class inclusions.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction broaden the empirical contribution from evidence that looping helps BFVP to benefits of looping and padding across several CFLs. The central resource bounds for general, unambiguous, and linear unambiguous CFLs, together with unpadded BFVP recognition, remain.

C2.justification: V3 adds an interpretation connecting items and slashed items to inside-outside probability computation and expands discussion of learnability. It also qualifies average-hard-attention approximation as non-universal and explicitly notes the unbounded-precision assumption of the cited Palindrome construction.

D1.justification: Appendix B substantially expands implementation specifications for the theoretical constructions: residual-stream slots, query/key/value choices, masks, initialization, scratch resets, and layer schedules are now explicit. Appendix A additionally identifies the learned linear input embedding used experimentally. These additions go well beyond the earlier construction sketches.

R1.justification: V3 adds related work on parallel parsing, transformer expressivity, and learnability, including Rytter (1987), Svete et al. (2026), and Borenstein et al. (2024). The Dyck expressivity attribution changes from Weiss et al. (2021) to Hayakawa and Sato (2024). The central research positioning remains.

P1.justification: Sections 3–4 are extensively rewritten and divided into algorithmic and transformer-construction subsections. Appendix B is reorganized and greatly elaborated, and discussion and conclusion become separate sections. Terminology, item notation, and explanatory prose are revised throughout.

P2.justification: V3 adds the postfix/residual-stream illustration in Figure 1 and replaces v2's Gorn-address tree with the before-and-after binarization diagram in Figure 2. Table 1 gains theorem references, and Table 2 changes from grouped ID/OOD columns to three model columns. The basic document layout remains.

improvement.justification: V3 improves exposition and addresses concrete weaknesses through the corrected centroid statement and compact binarization indexing. However, best-of-five reporting removes empirical uncertainty information. Its new Lemma B.3 also contains an update inconsistency: an unknown node with two known operands is made self-dependent, but the pebble rule updates only when that dependency's value is already known. V2 explicitly evaluated constant propagators directly. These theoretical and reporting drawbacks coexist with substantial clarification and corrections, leaving the net quality change uncertain.
